title: The Black Maria, the turning studio
hook: Edison's first film studio spun on a turntable to chase the sun.
peek: In 1893 Thomas Edison's team built a tar-papered shed in New Jersey to make the first films for his peep-show viewers. Its roof opened to the sky, and the whole building could be turned to follow the sun across the day.
lede: Early film stock needed a lot of light, and electric lamps of the 1890s were not bright enough. So at West Orange, New Jersey, Edison's assistant William Kennedy Laurie Dickson designed a studio that went to the light instead. Finished in 1893, the Black Maria had a roof that swung open and sat on a pivot, so the crew could rotate it to keep sunlight on the stage.

bullets.text: The building was covered in black tar paper inside and out, and it was cramped and stuffy. Staff said it looked like a police van, which were nicknamed Black Marias at the time, and the name stuck.

The films made there were short, often well under a minute, and were watched by one person at a time through Edison's Kinetoscope peep-show cabinet. The black walls made performers stand out sharply against the background.

Early subjects included three men acting out a day at the forge in Blacksmith Scene, and the strongman Eugen Sandow flexing for the camera. Vaudeville acts, dancers and Wild West performers came out to be filmed.
Edison's company stopped using the studio in the early 1900s and it was torn down. A full-size replica was built in 1954 and still stands at the Thomas Edison National Historical Park in West Orange.
